canberra.title: French burglars used ChatGPT to track down Canberra victims before stealing luxury items worth $2 million
canberra.snippet: Sitting overseas, a soon-to-be burglar from France used artificial intelligence (AI) to work out that a woman posting luxury-branded item...
canberra.content:
The burglars used AI tools like ChatGPT to help them commit their crime. Photo: Sanket Mishra.

Sitting overseas, a soon-to-be burglar from France used artificial intelligence (AI) to work out that a woman posting luxury-branded items on social media lived in Canberra.

He and his three co-offenders then flew to Australia, travelled to the ACT and stole almost $2 million worth of items from her home.

The four Frenchmen involved in the saga are 29-year-old Mohamed Naimi, 30-year-old Ilyes Abdelkader, 33-year-old Antoni Raymond Christian Charley Voisin and 38-year-old Mohamed Sophian Abdelkader.

All have pleaded guilty to charges of burglary and theft.

Newly obtained court documents show the victim used to post photos of the expensive luxury items she owned on her public social media account.

After the soon-to-be burglars learned of this, Ilyes Abdelkader trawled through the photos on her account and used AI to work out she lived in Canberra.

For example, AI informed him that one of her photos showed Telstra Tower in the background.

Utilising the AI tool ChatGPT, Ilyes Abdelkader then used the photos the woman posted on social media to work out which suburb she lived in.

He would later also use this AI tool to research the woman and her partner. In addition, he would search the internet for information on the school their child attended.

ACT Policing released these images of stolen items in December 2025, including this Hermes ring.

Hermes Gavroche ring.

Van Cleef Seoul necklace.

Patek Philippe watch.

Patek Philippe 40th anniversary watch.

The disputed Richard Mille RM88 Smiley watch.

On 7 October 2025, the four Frenchmen took a Jetstar flight from Thailand to Sydney. They rented a Mitsubishi Outlander at the airport, then drove to Canberra on 12 October.

The rental car was seen driving past the victims’ home numerous times two days later. The men also set up a camera in a tree opposite the home to surveil it.

The victims left their home late at night on 15 October. The burglars arrived within 15 minutes, and Ilyes Abdelkader and Voisin went inside, while Naimi and Mohamed Abdelkader waited in the car as lookouts.

Ilyes and Voisin used tree trunks to smash a window to break in. They then accessed a safe and stole 83 items, mostly from luxury brands such as Hermes, Chanel, Van Cleef & Arpels, and Rolex.

The stolen items included a pair of $47,000 earrings, a $78,000 handbag, an $80,000 bracelet, a $111,000 ring and a $166,000 ring.

There was also a $292,000 Hermes Tourbillon watch.

The four Frenchmen had driven out of the ACT within half an hour of the break-in. However, police tracked them all down and arrested them that same month.

The matter was scheduled to go to a disputed facts hearing in the ACT Supreme Court on Monday (7 September), as while the four men pleaded guilty, they disputed the original claim that the stolen items were worth up to $10 million.

But prosecutor Marcus Dyason said the matter had resolved and he tendered a copy of an agreed statement of facts to the court.

These documents show the stolen items were worth over $1,990,000 in total. Of this sum, about $915,000-worth of the goods were returned.

This means about $1 million worth of the items are yet to be recovered.

Originally, one of the stolen watches was said to be a limited-edition Richard Mille RM 88, which, according to several online listings, was estimated to be worth between $3 million and $ 5 million.

However, the agreed court documents state that the stolen item only “appeared to be an 88 Smiley watch”. The item has not been found, and the documents note that the prosecution was unable to prove it was genuine.

Justice Andrew Muller adjourned to 16 September to find a date for the men, all of whom remain in custody, to be sentenced.

canberra.title: Steel can’t skate over lost decade for ice sports, says Opposition
canberra.snippet: There’s no Bradbury gold medal at the end of this ice sports crash. The ACT Government blames the development partners. They blame ...
canberra.content:
Canberra Liberals leader Mark Parton and his deputy, Brindabella MLA Deborah Morris: “It’s a 100 per cent debacle.” Photos: Ian Bushnell.

There’s no Bradbury gold medal at the end of this ice sports crash.

The ACT Government blames the development partners. They blame the Tuggeranong location and site.

The Opposition blames the government.

The ice sports community is disappointed but insists it’s still in the race, suggesting the ACT had probably dodged a bullet not proceeding with a development partner more interested in an ice hockey stadium than other ice sports.

In November 2025, the Territory requested its preferred delivery partner, Cruachan/Pelligra, submit an updated, detailed proposal for the Greenway site.

This was provided on 13 January 2026, with Cruachan/Pelligra seeking more than double the $16.265 million government funding budgeted to deliver the proposed facility.

But Sport and Recreation Minister Chris Steel said the tender evaluation found a range of unacceptable risks, and the updated proposal did not represent value for money for the ACT.

Meanwhile, the funding committed to the project is being diverted to other sports in Tuggeranong in a bid to keep faith with voters and minimise recriminations.

The Tuggeranong ice sports saga goes back a decade and three elections, and even when the end was near, the government dragged it out months after it knew the jig was up.

Government official Rebecca Kelley told a press conference that the new tender evaluation process was completed in April and the previous sport minister, Yvette Berry, was aware of the outcome before she resigned in July.

Mr Steel fudged the timeline, and how much the development partners actually wanted, but the outcome is the same – the ice sports community and the government now go back to the drawing board to find a way forward.

Ice sports community spokesperson Sandi Logan said the community was profoundly disappointed but not surprised.

“We’ve not had a great deal of confidence in recent times in the proponents’ ideas and the proposals that they put up to amend the original concept of a community facility,” he said.

“If ever there was a demonstration of the need for probity and governance in a project, a major infrastructure project such as this, I think this one demonstrates it, and we’re in a way grateful that we’ll have another chance to come up with a better arrangement, a better partnership, and a better opportunity for the community to pursue ice sports in Canberra.”

“Unacceptable risks”: Sport and Recreation Minister Chris Steel, flanked by government official Rebecca Kelley.

The Opposition called it a decade of deceit, delay and disorder, and at the end the government had nothing to show for it.

Canberra Liberals Leader Mark Parton said it was a 100 per cent debacle that was all the government’s fault.

Mr Parton said the development partners had issues with the viability of the Tuggeranong site from the start.

He said the message for development proponents was that dealing with this government carried a risk.

“I can understand that perception, and it’s not a perception which is going to help us as taxpayers,” he said.

Liberal sports spokesperson James Milligan said there was a desperate need for a twin ice sheet facility in the Territory and the Liberals were committed to delivering one in partnership with the private sector.

“We would need to consider the level of commitment … but I’m sure that we’ll get a better deal and deliver a better outcome by working with the private industry to deliver an ice rink in a suitable location that doesn’t necessarily require such a large investment from the government,” he said.

All eyes are now on the Phillip Ice Skating Centre, owned by Geocon, which eventually plans to build an apartment building on the site.

But Mr Steel said the Territory plan still required an ice facility on that site until an alternative was available.

Independent MLA Fiona Carrick called on Geocon to invest in the Phillip facility for the ice sports community.

That’s something Mr Steel would support.

“We’d hope that there’d be interest potentially in delivering something, whether that’s at the current site in Phillip or another site,” he said.

Mr Steel indicated that the needs of ice hockey had diverged from the initial ice sports proposal, with the Canberra Brave’s successful move to the AIS Arena and calls for a larger stadium to support what proponents are calling Canberra’s new boom winter sport.

“We’ve already seen the Brave come forward and suggest that they need an even larger facility than what they have at AIS, which is the largest in the country, to support their needs,” he said.

“We want to work with the ice sports community to understand what their needs are and what opportunities there could be to make sure that they have the facilities that are required now and into the future.”

The siting of the proposed ice sports area in Tuggeranong was motivated in part by a desire to win favour with Brindabella voters, but that has now backfired.

A fired-up Labor MLA Taimus Werner-Gibbings laid into the development partners, but he also made it clear that Tuggeranong again felt shortchanged.

He already has a list of projects that the now-available $16 million could fund.

“Over the next few months, I will improve and finalise the list by holding many more discussions in Tuggeranong about the results of the new sports infrastructure survey,” he said.

“Tuggeranong is sick of waiting for our fair share. The government must outline its plan, commit to a timeline and get on with delivering the sports infrastructure our community needs and deserves.”

Bean MP David Smith may even have some federal money to help out, given he is sitting on a wafer-thin margin.

“I would welcome the opportunity to work with Minister Steel and the ACT Government to deliver the major sporting facility the people of Canberra’s south deserve,” Mr Smith said.

canberra.title: One Nation has a plan to let Aussies tap into super before retirement
canberra.snippet: One Nation wants to give Australians paying rent or a mortgage the freedom to divert 3 per cent of their future compulsory superannuation...
canberra.content:
One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce and Pauline Hanson explain their new superannuation policy. Photo: Facebook.

One Nation wants to give Australians paying rent or a mortgage the freedom to divert 3 per cent of their future compulsory superannuation contributions to their bank accounts to help with the cost of living.

They would only be able to do it for a maximum of three years, in a measure the party’s leader, Pauline Hanson, says will help those who are struggling to pay their bills right now.

“People are working hard and still struggling to get ahead. Interest rates keep rising; rents keep climbing; groceries, power bills, petrol and insurance are taking more and more out of the family budget,” Senator Hanson said on Monday (7 September).

“Inflation is hurting Australian families and Labor’s economic incompetence is making life harder. One Nation wants to give people some breathing room.

“If you are paying rent or a mortgage on your home, One Nation will allow you to choose to receive one quarter of your future compulsory super contributions in your take-home pay for up to three years.

“Super is currently 12 per cent of your wages. Your employer will still pay the full 12 per cent.

“But if you take the boost, one quarter of this contribution will be paid directly to you by your super fund.

“And you won’t be slugged with your normal income-tax rate on it either.”

Under the policy, the money would be taxed at the same low rate it would have received in super.

For a full-time worker earning about $90,500, it would mean about $2,300 a year after tax extra in their pockets – or $44 a week.

For a working couple earning $168,000 between them, it would be about $4,300 a year after tax, or $82 a week.

“If they feel that they want to access that and get one quarter of their superannuation, they’re putting away each week, like I said, $44 can mean that people can pay their bills, their electricity, put food on the table or get medical attention,” Senator Hanson said.

“So that means a lot to a lot of people.”

Treasurer Jim Chalmers immediately panned the idea, saying it would make Australians worse off in retirement.

“It’s now beyond doubt that any Coalition government with One Nation in it will cut your super,” he said.

“This means less money and less economic security for millions of Australian workers.

“This will end superannuation as we know it and make millions of Australians poorer as a consequence.

“One Nation is anti‑super because One Nation is anti‑worker. You can’t be pro‑worker and anti‑superannuation.”

Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek said: “It’s obvious One Nation wants you to raid your super instead of getting a pay increase. We support higher wages and better super when you retire.”

The One Nation leader denied that she intended to shut down the superannuation system.

“I believe that these people need a helping hand,” she said.

“Now our Treasurer Jim Chalmers is saying that I want to shut the super down.

“That’s the furthest thing from the truth. I’m not intending to shut super down.”

Despite the Treasurer suggesting the Coalition was in cahoots with One Nation on superannuation policy, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said Senator Hanson’s proposal raises more questions than it answers.

“There are all sorts of questions that I haven’t seen answered on it,” Mr Taylor said.

“Is that money going to get access to the tax concessions of superannuation? How will paid parental leave superannuation be dealt with in this? Will this contribute to the concessional caps?

“I mean, what we see with these policy announcements constantly is no detail, and the detail really matters.”

One Nation’s treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce can’t see why either of the major parties would have any issue with the policy, suggesting it was only tweaking at the edges of how superannuation is managed.

“This is not a seismic shift in administration. It’s a change in attitude – that if you’re doing it tough, you get some of your own money back,” he said.

“What we are doing here is giving people back some of their own money from the future, not taking it out of their current balance, but some of their own money in the future.

“And what we have to realise is that superannuation is not a national asset. It’s [an] individual’s asset.

“If you lose your house… you’re going to be vastly worse off than the benefit you’ll get from that margin of investment over the longer term.

“I just can’t see why the government’s got a problem with this.”

canberra.title: Canberra man accused of abusing stepdaughter granted bail, but must leave ACT
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse. A man was given several hours to leave the ACT after he was granted bail ove...
canberra.content:
7 September 2026

A 40-year-old man faces eight charges accusing him of abusing his stepdaughter. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse.

A man was given several hours to leave the ACT after he was granted bail over allegations of sexually assaulting his own stepdaughter.

The 40-year-old, who is not named to avoid identifying his family, was handed eight charges before the ACT Magistrates Court granted him bail to live in Queensland on Monday (7 September).

An ACT Policing spokesperson said it was alleged the man sexually abused the girl in Canberra for eight months, between December 2025 and August 2026.

The allegations were reported to police on the weekend before the man was arrested that afternoon.

He was charged with four counts of committing an act of indecency with a young person under special care, two counts of sexual intercourse with a young person under special care and one count each of incest and grooming.

But on Monday, the court heard he had been charged incorrectly as the act of indecency charges actually related to allegations of sexual assault.

He applied for bail, which the prosecution opposed.

“The real risk is the power imbalance relationship that he has with the complainant,” the prosecutor said.

The prosecutor said the girl had yet to finish her interview with the police. Also, the investigation was ongoing, and police suspected more allegations would be made.

But the man’s lawyer, Eimear Silk of Legal Aid, said her client had no criminal history and a consistent employment record.

Ms Silk accepted the allegations against him were very serious and the alleged risk he posed was to his family members. But she said he could move to Queensland if he were granted bail, which would put a considerable distance between him and his family.

Magistrate Alexandra Burt noted the stepdaughter had been suffering psychological distress, allegedly related to the man’s actions.

But she said the lack of prior criminal history was an important factor in her decision, and she was not satisfied that the risks of releasing him were so high as to justify his detention.

The magistrate granted bail on conditions, including that the man not contact or approach the stepdaughter or other members of his family, and that he leave the ACT by 5 pm on Monday afternoon.

No pleas were entered. The matter was adjourned to October.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

You can also submit an online report about a historical sexual assault allegation for incidents that occurred more than six months ago.

canberra.title: Man allegedly planned to meet 14-year-old girl at sportsground
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse. Police allege a man was planning to meet up with a 14-year-old girl at a Can...
canberra.content:
7 September 2026

Police were told a man had allegedly been messaging a 14-year-old girl over social media. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse.

Police allege a man was planning to meet up with a 14-year-old girl at a Canberra sportsground when he was instead picked up at the location by their officers.

Rami Saleh, a 23-year-old from the ACT suburb of Farrer, has said he will fight the three charges he has been handed over the allegations.

In August 2026, police were told a man had allegedly been engaging in sexual messaging with a 14-year-old girl via social media, an ACT Policing spokesperson said.

This report resulted in officers from the Sexual Assault and Child Abuse Team starting an investigation.

In addition, it is alleged the man provided cash and alcohol to the girl.

Then, on Friday night (4 September), it is alleged that Mr Saleh went to Chapman Oval under the belief that he was meeting the 14-year-old in person.

Instead, police arrested him in the sportsground’s carpark. He was charged with grooming a young person, using a carriage service for child abuse material and supplying liquor to a young person.

“Phones in his possession were seized and these will be forensically examined to determine if further offences are applicable,” an ACT Policing spokesperson said.

Mr Saleh remained in custody over the weekend before briefly facing the ACT Magistrates Court on Monday (7 September).

His lawyer, Michael Kukulies-Smith of Kamy Saeedi Law, said his client would not apply for bail but would enter not-guilty pleas to all three charges.

He also said the allegations were not related to family violence.

Prosecutor Hal Tilemann then said his office anticipated more charges would be laid.

Magistrate Alexandra Burt recorded Mr Saleh’s not guilty pleas, remanded him in custody and adjourned the matter to 22 October for a pre-hearing mention.

australia.title: Radiohead announce 2027 tour with shows in Australia and Japan
australia.snippet: UK band will play 16 shows across Perth, Melbourne and Sydney, as well as five shows in Saitama Radiohead will return to Australia to pla...
australia.content:
Radiohead will return to Australia to play 16 shows across three cities next year, marking the band’s first tour of the country in 15 years.

On Monday afternoon, the British rock band unveiled the itinerary for its May 2027 tour, which also includes five shows in Japan.

The series of shows will kick off at Perth’s RAC Arena on 3 May for four performances in the city. This will be followed by six shows at Melbourne’s Rod Laver Arena and Sydney’s Afterpay Arena.

The band last toured Australia after their 2011 album the King of Limbs, although frontman Thom Yorke visited Australia for solo shows in 2024. During a Melbourne performance, Yorke walked off stage after being heckled by a pro-Palestine protester in the crowd. He returned a few minutes later to perform his final song of the evening, Radiohead’s 1997 hit Karma Police.

Last year, Radiohead reunited after seven years for a string of shows in European cities.

The band will also return to Japan for the first time in 19 years with five concerts at the GMO Arena Saitama near Tokyo.

The band has not recorded a studio album since 2016’s A Moon Shaped Pool. But the absence of new material has not quelled demand, with a frenzied rush for tickets when the shows were announced.

Radiohead first toured Australia in 1994 after the band’s debut album Pablo Honey, which contained their breakthrough hit Creep.

Fans can register interest for tickets to the Australian shows on an online portal – run by co-promoter Frontier Touring – that opened on Monday evening. It will create a ballot-like process to “help give fans fair access to tickets and minimise automated and unauthorised purchases.”

Tickets are capped at four for each city the band is performing in, the portal said.

“There’s no benefit to registering earlier. Every completed registration received by the deadline will be treated equally,” the website said.

Registration closes on Thursday at 5pm AEST. Successful registrants will be emailed with next steps from Friday and given a chance to buy tickets next week.

australia.title: Australia’s top bureaucrats want to block sharing of clips from parliament on social media to save them from ‘ridicule’
australia.snippet: Secretaries board concerned material posted without proper context as Greens warn ban could result in lack of transparency Get our breaki...
australia.content:
The nation’s top bureaucrats want the Albanese government to ban video footage from parliamentary hearings being edited and shared on social media, in an extraordinary attempt to stop online ridicule and abuse.

But the Greens say highly paid public service chiefs shouldn’t be allowed to control footage from open parliamentary hearings, warning the proposed controls would limit a key tool of government transparency.

The secretaries board – made up of the heads of government departments and chaired by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet boss, Steven Kennedy – said they were concerned about material from hearings being presented online without proper context.

Politicians and political parties doing so exposed officials to “ridicule, hostility and abuse”, the board said.

“Recognising the evidence provided to a committee is on the public record, these officials have not consented to a subsequent use of their image, or its use by parliamentarians and their political parties for party-political purposes,” the board said in a submission published on Monday.

“In our view, the use of officials’ likenesses and their evidence in this way has the potential to be harmful both to the individual and the public sector as a whole.”

If the recommendations are not taken up, the board called for rules that would stop videos being edited or having captions added. Politicians would also be stopped from sharing content or commentary that targets individual officials for ridicule or harassment.

Calling for footage of full hearings and transcripts to be made available instead of clips, and for comments to be disabled, the board said its proposal would ensure “that scrutiny remains focused on evidence, administration and accountability rather than becoming personal”.

The proposal also includes concerns that members of parliament might not have a clear understanding of the role and responsibilities of public servants, when compared with government ministers. The board called for clearer explanation, including for newer MPs.

The push comes after the defence department deputy secretary Celia Perkins told a parliamentary hearing last week that public servants giving evidence did not consent to footage being shared on social media.

“They do not consent to the reposting of our evidence to social media sites or the reproduction of our likenesses for the purposes outside the framework of the parliament and the transparent public proceedings of this committee,” Perkins said.

The Senate foreign affairs, defence and trade committee rejected Perkins’ request on the advice of the Senate clerk.

Greens senator Steph Hodgins-May told Guardian Australia that members of the public had the right to see footage from hearings into government scrutiny.

“Bureaucrats shouldn’t get to decide where to draw the line on parliamentary scrutiny, particularly when they’re the ones being scrutinised,” she said.

“Of course debate should be respectful, but restricting what parliamentarians can post from public proceedings is not the answer.

“This looks like an attempt to take the teeth out of parliamentary scrutiny. Australians deserve more transparency and accountability, not less. And frankly, if this scrutiny wasn’t having an impact, they wouldn’t be so worried about it.”

The secretaries board includes all departmental chiefs, the Australian Public Service commissioner and the chief executive of the National Indigenous Australians Agency.

australia.title: Liberal operatives discussed whether to buy Porsche or Ferrari with developer’s payments, Icac hears
australia.snippet: Rightwing NSW powerbrokers are alleged to have received illegal political donations from fugitive developer Follow our Australia news liv...
australia.content:
Two Liberal operatives traded photos and messages about whether to buy a Porsche or a Ferrari with payments they received for Toplace projects they got approved via a New South Wales government fast-track development process.

The Independent Commission Against Corruption on Monday heard more evidence from lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood, a principal of Beckington Consulting, who is alleged to have shared in $2m in payments from the fugitive developer Jean Nassif, owner of the now collapsed Toplace.

Greenwood along with Charles Perrottet, a rightwing political powerbroker and brother of the former premier Dominic Perrottet, and Christian Ellis, a fellow conservative rightwing Liberal, are alleged to have received illegal political donations.

Charles Perrottet and Greenwood have denied taking illegal political donations. Ellis is overseas and is not expected to give evidence during the hearings.

Dominic Perrottet is not a person of interest in Icac’s inquiry and is not accused of any wrongdoing.

Icac alleges that the payments were used to fund political outcomes, including the removal of the Hills shire council and attempts to remove the building commissioner David Chandler, who had placed prohibition orders on Nassif’s developments due to defects.

The counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer has said the payments were split three ways between the trio.

Charles Perrottet and Greenwood attended a meeting in April 2020 with Nassif and around the same time Greenwood and Ellis had a text exchange in which they traded pictures of cars they desired. Greenwood sent a picture of a Porsche 911.

Ellis replied: “I don’t know. The top of the range one. It’s just insane.”

Greenwood: “There’s something about a red Ferrari always.”

Ellis: “That’s true too. That Ferrari is very nice, very very nice.”

Greenwood: “It costs about 280, same as that Porsche.”

Ellis: “Ferrari. Definitely.”

Dwyer asked: “You ultimately settle on a Porsche, is that right?”

“Yes, but not the $280,000 one,” Greenwood replied.

Dwyer said this exchange indicated that at the 24 April meeting between Nassif, Charles Perrottet and Greenwood was where huge payments for getting Nassif’s developments approved were discussed.

Greenwood agreed that the trio were offered $1m per project if they were accepted for the fast track.

He said there were potentially five projects including 189 Macquarie Street in Parramatta, Garthowen in Castle Hill, O’Riordan Street in Mascot, a Cherrybrook project, and perhaps one at either Clyde or Box Hill, which might have yielded project payments.

Icac has failed to find any paperwork showing evidence of the project payments.

That was because Nassif was not easy to work for, Greenwood said. He often paid late and did not believe in paperwork.

“That’s not how Jean operated,” Greenwood said.

Greenwood said a note about the arrangement had once been stored in the back of the Toplace general manager, Larissa Mouawad’s phone case and he noticed it at a meeting in 2020.

It was on a pink piece of note paper, folded in half.

“Fuschia, purple-pink,” was how Greenwood described it.

Greenwood said he was alarmed about Mouawad having the note and it was later reclaimed by either Nassif, or his lawyer Sharanan Maheswaran. He had not seen it since, he told Icac.

Taken through the accounts by Dwyer, Greenwood agreed that the book-keeping at Beckington and paperwork was chaotic but denied it was because they were attempting to disguise payments that were made for political outcomes.

Greenwood said they often experienced difficulties getting payment from Nassif, and that Charles Perrottet was sometimes used to help prompt Nassif to pay.

Charles Perrottet has denied that he did work for the developer. He said he offered “advice” to Greenwood and Ellis and they offered to reward him by paying his wife, Anita, via her company Macquarie Consulting.

In evidence last week, Charles Perrotett explained his regular contact with Nassif as just helping out his friends to get paid.

‘Dark arts’

Later on Monday, counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer, put to Greenwood that Beckinton stopped being official lobbyist for the collapsed developer, Toplace, so it could concentrate on the “dark arts” of political manoeuvering from November 2020.

Greenwood was one of the directors of Beckington.

Dwyer asked about the engagement of Premier National, another Liberal aligned lobbying group, which was associated with the moderate faction of the Liberal party, as the public face of Toplace’s lobbying efforts.

On 8 November 2020 it became the lobbyist for Toplace on 8 November, on the NSW parliament’s official lobbyist register, while Beckington removed Toplace as a client on 10 November.

Dwyer took Greenwood to a series of text messages in September 2020 where Greenwood said he “joked” with his business partner, Christian Ellis, why Greenwood was not present at a meeting with Toplace boss, Jean Nassif.

Greenwood suggested saying he was exhausted from “managing the recruits” and that “Elliott has offered them double to recruit for him”.

David Elliott was the Baulkham Hills MP and a political rival of the conservative right, who was hated by Nassif because he was perceived as opposing Toplace developments.

“These were just jokes,” Greenwood said, when asked whether these were evidence of their activities to stack branches in the Hills area.

“But what you’re actually doing here is explaining your strategy, isn’t it? You’ve got Premier National going in the front door as the formal lobbyist, but what you’re doing is the dark arts, on behalf of Jean Nassif, isn’t that correct?” Dwyer asked.

Greenwood denied this was the case.

Nassif is now a fugitive in Lebanon. He has agreed to give evidence by video link next Monday, though he pulled out of a similar arrangement last week.

The inquiry continues.

australia.title: Coalition targets Labor over ‘plummeting’ Sydney house prices – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here One Nation has come up with a plan to give peop...
australia.content:
Are house prices ‘softening’ or ‘plummeting’?

The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, says Sydney house prices are “plummeting so fast that they are on track for the biggest crash in 40 years” in a question to the government.

The housing minister, Clare O’Neil, says the government was transparent about the changes in the budget, with Treasury modelling suggesting there will be 75,000 new owner occupiers and a “small and temporary slowing in house price growth”.

House prices grew 400% in the past 25 years, she says:

[Wilson] is accurate in one sense that house prices are softening across the country … this is the fourth time that we have seen this occur in a decade in our country.

Key events

  • 5h ago

    Good morning

What we learned today, Monday 7 September

That’s where we’ll leave our live coverage for today!

Before we go, let’s take a look at the day’s top headlines:

  • The parents of Australian brothers Callum and Jake Robinson, who were killed in Mexico in 2024, will fly to Ensenada to attend the aggravated homicide trial of their accused killers.

  • Two more Australians will join humanitarian and rescue efforts in the devastating Nepal-Tibet floods, as 36 Australians are among the nearly 5,000 people who remain unaccounted for.

  • One Nation has come up with a plan to give people their superannuation earlier, reducing the amount they’ll have at retirement in exchange for a short-term cash boost. But the super industry says it would be “economically disastrous” and stoke inflation and both Labor and the Liberal party have said they don’t support the policy.

  • New laws being introduced in NSW aim to tackle organised crime by giving police more power and creating a new aggravated offence for conspiracy to commit gang-related murder.

  • More than 200 workers at Bathla Group have been stood down as the administrator of the embattled property developer seeks emergency funds to stave off a company-wide collapse.

  • The Greens have accused the NSW government of failing to tackle gambling harms after new data showed residents lost a record $2.38bn on poker machines in the last quarter.

  • Queensland police said two people have died after a light aircraft plunged on to a property at Chambers Flat in Logan, south of Brisbane.

That’s all for today, we’ll see you tomorrow to do it all over again!

Victorian Greens call for major tech companies to compensate residents affected by existing datacentres

The Victorian Greens have called on the government to require major tech companies to compensate residents affected by existing datacentres for noise, pollution and falling property values through a levy.

It comes as cabinet meet today to consider restrictions on the industry, amid increasing community opposition to the expansion of datacentres across the state. The debate has seen the country’s largest electricity distributor, Jemena, halt connections to new datacentres, the Age reports.

In a letter to the artificial intelligence and digital economy minister, Anthony Carbines, the party has laid out its “urgent demands to protect communities from Labor’s reckless datacentre rush”.

Among the demands, the Greens also want an immediate moratorium on new AI datacentre approvals and construction in the absence of legislation, and prohibitions on new datacentres on Melbourne’s green wedges and other land of significant agricultural importance.

The Greens’ AI and datacentres spokesperson, Dr Sarah Mansfield, said:

Datacentre corporations and the global tech giants stand to make billions in profit, while Victorian families bear the costs – noise, pollution and falling property values.

If these corporations damage people’s homes, health or quality of life, they must be forced to compensate them in full.

Cabinet has an opportunity today to finally put communities ahead of tech-bro billionaires. Anything short of compensation, a moratorium and proper exclusion zones will be another capitulation to the datacentre lobby.

Benita Kolovos

Victorian premier plans to pass work from home laws this week

Victoria’s premier, Ben Carroll, says the government will introduce amendments to its work from home bill and pass it through parliament this week.

Before she was deposed as leader, Carroll’s predecessor Jacinta Allan had announced plans to legislate the right to work from home two days a week for those who can “reasonably” do so and had secured bipartisan support for the bill.

But one of Carroll’s first acts as premier – after a media blitz by business groups – was to announce he would push back the bill’s commencement from 1 September to July 2027. The bill has then been sitting towards the bottom of the upper house notice paper after passing through the lower house.

This afternoon, he posted on social media that he had made some “sensible amendments” to the bill and expects it to pass this week:

We’re going to pass the right to work from home laws this week. Work from home works. That’s the message I’ve heard loud and clear. But these laws need to work for business too, because the reality is, if it’s not practical for employers, the laws won’t last. So I’ve made some sensible amendments to these laws to make them practical and affordable for businesses, while preserving the right for workers.

Carroll has previously signalled he was open to amendments that would ensure businesses don’t have to foot the bill for home office equipment and other costs.

Luca Ittimani

What would One Nation’s super policy mean for you and your retirement?

One Nation’s new super policy proposes splitting the 12% compulsory super payment so that 3% could be used prior to retirement. Critics say it would just push up inflation.

For a breakdown on all of this and what it means, we’ve laid it out for you here:

Hastie says One Nation’s super policy a distraction from internal problems

Coalition frontbencher Andrew Hastie has called One Nation’s proposed policy to divert superannuation payments into workers’ pay packets a distraction from the party’s other issues.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Hastie questioned whether the policy would work.

I think Pauline Hanson is trying to address a real cost-of-living pressure for Australians. If you look at real wages since the pandemic, they have crashed and not recovered. Go to the outer metropolitan parts of this country, people are doing it really tough, no matter what state or territory.

One Nation are seeking to address cost-of-living pressure, that’s great. The question is, will it work? And that is a question for which I have not seen the modelling or the costing.

The comments come as One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, continues to attract scrutiny over allegations made against him by an ex-partner about alleged drug use.

Hastie said:

Warren Pickering, the One Nation candidate, has questions to answer about his past, and Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce have questions to answer about what they have known about his past. You could argue this is a magician’s trick.

Pickering has rejected his ex-partner’s claims as “false”. “They are extremely hurtful and I just hope the public can see through them,” he said in a statement, according to The Australian.

Two people dead after light plane crash south of Brisbane

Police have confirmed two people have died following reports of a light aircraft crash after the plane plunged on to a property at Chambers Flat in Logan after 11am on Monday.

The crash sparked a fast-moving grass fire which saw at least a dozen fire trucks and multiple crews work to contain the blaze, which burned close to a farmhouse before being brought under control about 12.50pm.

Police have yet to release further information surrounding the circumstances of the pair’s deaths and are awaiting further details.

At a press conference, Ch Supt Mel Adams from Queensland police said officers are in the process of identifying and contacting the deceased’s next of kin.

It was a very confronting scene as you can imagine. So, our care at the moment is to our emergency service responders and of course the family when we can make contact with them and notify them.

Police have called on any witnesses of the incident to come forward to assist in investigations.

We’re still searching for witnesses in that matter. So I reiterate my call to the public. Please contact police if you have information to share in relation to this tragic incident today.

Boy speared in back during unrest in remote NT community

Police say a 14-year-old boy has been speared in the back as tensions rise between family groups in a remote Top End community, AAP reports.

The spearing allegedly occurred in Ngukurr, one of the largest Indigenous communities in the Northern Territory’s Roper Gulf region, with a population of just over 1,000 people.

The community unrest started on Friday evening, with police receiving reports of a large disturbance between two family groups in the township. Police said in a statement:

A number of people were allegedly armed with weapons during the disturbance.

No injuries were reported at the time.

More reports of disturbances involving weapons were received after tensions escalated on Saturday afternoon. Police said:

At around 5.35pm, police received a report that a 14-year-old boy had been speared in the middle of his back.

Officers went to the local health clinic where they spoke with the boy and his family. Police said:

He was subsequently medically evacuated by CareFlight for further treatment and remains in a stable condition.

Officers are working with local leaders and elders in a bid to prevent further violence.

Light plane plunges into Queensland paddock, sparks grass fire

A light aircraft has plunged into a rural property in Queensland, sparking a fast‑moving grass fire and a massive emergency response, with grave fears held for the people on board, AAP reports.

The plane went down on a paddock south of Brisbane after 11am on Monday, with shocked residents raising the alarm as smoke billowed across paddocks.

Crews were called to a grass fire just after 11am and arrived to find plane debris scattered on the Chambers Flat property and flames racing through dry grass across an area about 300 by 400 metres, authorities said.

At least a dozen fire trucks and multiple crews worked to contain the blaze, which burned close to a farmhouse before being brought under control about 12.50pm.

No homes were damaged.

Police have cordoned off the crash site and have yet to confirm how many people were on board or whether anyone has been injured.

Paramedics and firefighters remain at the scene as investigators work to piece together what caused the accident.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau has been notified and will investigate the crash.

Arts Centre Melbourne workers take industrial action for the first time

Stephanie Convery

Workers at Australia’s largest performing arts venue, Arts Centre Melbourne, have taken industrial action for the first time in its history, with multiple work stoppages delaying performances last week, and more expected to come.

Ushers, food and beverage attendants, stage managers, ticketing staff, programmers, electricians, technicians, and other unionised employees of the VVictorian government-run Arts Centre walked out of the building as audiences took their seats for five shows last week.

The workers are calling for a 7% annual pay rise to make up for wage stagnation since 2022. The previous enterprise agreement saw wages increase by 1% every six months, and many of the band 1 wages in the expired agreement are now below the national minimums. The Arts Centre had to increase affected workers’ pay after the recent minimum wage review to ensure they were not paid less than the national baseline. The Arts Centre told the Guardian none of its workers were paid below minimum wage, and has offered a pay rise of 3% annually, the equivalent of the Victorian government wages cap.

Members of MEAA, the Community and Public Sector Union Victoria, and the Electrical Trades Union have been bargaining with the Arts Centre on a new enterprise agreement since March.

Footage posted to social media by the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance (MEAA) last week showed audiences applauding a worker announcement explaining that the delay to the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra’s performance of How to Train Your Dragon 2 was caused by industrial action.

The Symphony Orchestra Musicians’ Association, part of MEAA, has also expressed its support for the striking workers.

A union petition that had nearly 3000 signatures at the time of writing called on the Victorian government to “increase funding to Arts Centre Melbourne and give workers a real pay increase that reverses years of real wage decline”, linking worker pay to the broader issue of cultural funding.

A spokesperson for Arts Centre Melbourne said the organisation respected workers’ rights to take lawful industrial action, and continued to bargain in good faith with union representatives to reach an agreement that was “fair and financially sustainable outcome that is consistent with the Victorian Government Wages Policy”.

The spokesperson said:

Arts Centre Melbourne has reached agreement with unions on a range of detailed conditions within the proposed Enterprise Agreement. The main outstanding issue is wage increases … During this period of industrial action, our priority is to minimise disruption for presenters, artists, and audiences, while maintaining a safe working environment for our team.

Tory Shepherd

That’s all from me, Achol Arok will guide you through the rest of the afternoon’s news.

Nationals call on government to ‘scrap the cap’ on veterans’ allied health services

Nationals MP Michael McCormack calls on the government to “scrap the cap” on veterans’ allied health services.

Albanese says the government is consulting on the changes; increasing the fees paid to allied health professionals; removing the need for veterans to get a new referral every 12 months; and making further care available if there is a clinical need beyond that $5,000 cap.

The existing cap is 12 allied health visits before a veteran needs a referral. Albanese says the new cap of $5,000 will allow more visits.

The resources minister, Madeleine King, wraps up question time with an ode to Australia’s critical minerals capabilities.

Greens: Beetaloo fracking a ‘giant climate bomb’

Greens MP Elizabeth Watson-Brown asks the prime minister if he supports the resources minister, Madeleine King, on the fracking of the Beetaloo basin, describing it as a “plan to ignite this giant climate bomb”.

Anthony Albanese says he supports his ministers as well as “real action on climate change”. He says:

Unless you have firming capacity, you won’t have the expansion of renewables that is important for the transition.

Enforcement and compliance focus in tobacco war, Chalmers says

Nationals MP Llew O’Brien is demanding a yes/no answer on whether the government will rule out any reduction in the tobacco excise.

“The government’s priority is to deal with this as an enforcement issue, a compliance issue, a law enforcement issue,” Jim Chalmers says.

In answer to objections from the opposition about the relevance of his answer, the speaker, Milton Dick, says he can’t force the treasurer to say yes or no.

Tim Wilson booted from chamber

Jim Chalmers is quoting the shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson – who was just booted from the chamber for being rowdy – saying he would “like to slow the growth in the price of housing”.

“Then he says he wrote a whole book about it,” Chalmers says.

And we’re back to another demand the government join the Coalition to “crush the organised crime gangs”.

The health minister, Mark Butler, talks about the opposition increasing the tobacco excise by far more than Labor did when they were in power.

“And they trousered every single dollar,” he says.

He says Queensland and South Australia have put extra enforcement powers in place and there’s a “completely different picture” to that playing out in NSW and Victoria.

Taylor says tobacco excise cut would ‘crush’ organised crime

Now to the tobacco excise wars, sparked by the explosion in illegal tobacco.

Opposition leader Angus Taylor talks about the firebombing of small businesses and the need to “crush the organised crime gangs”. The opposition wants to cut the excise cut on cigarettes, so they would be more competitive on price.

Leader of the house Tony Burke says “the last thing this parliament should ever do is outsource its health policy to organised crime”.

It has to be dealt with through law enforcement, he says, adding:

They know all too well that the exact impact of what they are proposing would be an increase in tobacco consumption in Australia.

Katter calls for income splitting

Crossbench MP Bob Katter asks the treasurer about the cost-of-living crisis. He talks about the “appalling inequality” in the disposable income between those with children and “dinks” (double income, no kids).

Income splitting is the answer, he says, “while a birthing payment will help arrest Australia’s plunging birthrates”.

Jim Chalmers says a similar proposal was costed and it found it would cost the nation more than $12bn over the forward estimates and would “primarily benefit higher wealth and income couples”:

[It would] cost the budget substantially, while denying the people it’s designed to help.

Income splitting would create a tax transfer system that encourages economic dependence, reduces initiatives for women’s workforce participation [and] would risk unwinding some of the gains that we’ve made as a country.

Are house prices ‘softening’ or ‘plummeting’?

The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, says Sydney house prices are “plummeting so fast that they are on track for the biggest crash in 40 years” in a question to the government.

The housing minister, Clare O’Neil, says the government was transparent about the changes in the budget, with Treasury modelling suggesting there will be 75,000 new owner occupiers and a “small and temporary slowing in house price growth”.

House prices grew 400% in the past 25 years, she says:

[Wilson] is accurate in one sense that house prices are softening across the country … this is the fourth time that we have seen this occur in a decade in our country.

It's question time

After a moment of silence for Nepal, question time is up and running.

Up first is Angus Taylor, who asks Anthony Albanese about comments from the Property Council about the government’s taxes being “a ram raid on house prices”.

Albanese says the budget made no changes for people who already negatively gear property, and that investors are “borrowing to build more new homes than ever before”, citing a Herald Sun report and ABS data:

Going forward, negative gearing and the 50% capital gains tax can still be used for investment properties, but only on new builds, so when people choose to invest in housing, they’re not investing in their future wealth and assets, they’re investing in the future wealth and assets of the nation.

australia.title: One Nation says renters and mortgage holders should have early access to their super. Is it a good idea?
australia.snippet: The party proposes splitting the 12% compulsory super payment so that 3% could be used prior to retirement. Critics say it would just pus...
australia.content:
One Nation wants to let renters and mortgage holders take money from their superannuation to boost their pay packets.

The super industry says it would be “economically disastrous” and stoke inflation and both Labor and the Liberal party have said they don’t support the policy. But economists say the superannuation system needs reform.

How does early access work?

Employers pay 12% of workers’ earnings into their super accounts, where it is taxed at just 15% instead of their personal income tax rate.

At the moment, you can only get early access to the money in your super account for a set of specific purposes. People who have been paid income support for six consecutive months and cannot pay for urgent living expenses can apply for up to $10,000 every 12 months.

The Morrison government offered broader super releases in 2020 when it let people withdraw up to $20,000 if they were in hardship due to the Covid-19 crisis. Economists found large sums withdrawn were spent on gambling and shopping, while the Super Members Council (SMC) estimated about 725,000 Australians completely emptied their accounts.

One Nation is proposing far wider access. All renters and mortgage holders would be given the option to split their 12% payments into 9% for their super account and 3% to go back to their bank account, still at the low 15% tax rate.

About two in every three Australian households are renting or have a mortgage. One Nation estimates about 7 million people would be eligible.

There would be no other conditions and the money could be spent on anything, not just housing costs. Those who opted in would only get the split payments for a maximum of three years.

How would One Nation’s proposal affect you?

One Nation says the early release would mean a full-time worker earning $90,500 a year would get about $2,300 in their pocket that would otherwise have gone to their super account. That’s $44 a week.

But the SMC has estimated a typical 30-year-old worker on that income would end up $25,000 poorer by retirement if they opted in to the One Nation plan.

Barnaby Joyce, the One Nation MP, admitted the party had not modelled what the policy would cost workers in retirement.

“I can come back tomorrow with that,” he told a News24 host on Monday.

Poorer retirees would force the government to spend more on the age pension. The SMC estimated the Covid-era withdrawals, where 3 million Australians took out nearly $38bn, would cost taxpayers up to $85bn by the end of the century.

Asked on Monday about the prospect of higher pension spending, Pauline Hanson said: “I would rather see them get that help and assistance that they need now, not later in life.”

How would it affect the economy?

More cash in workers’ pockets today could help Australians handle the cost of living. Inflation is high at 3.5%, while wage growth is falling behind at 3.2% a year. The proposal would effectively lift wages by 3%, putting income growth ahead of price rises.

But it would also mean more money flowing through the economy when the Reserve Bank is trying to take money out by lifting interest rates. Strong household spending is one of the factors expected to increase inflation.

The Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia chief executive, Mary Delahunty, said the proposal would be “economically disastrous”.

“This policy would push up inflation and make people poorer in retirement,” Delahunty said.

Hanson has claimed the proposal is “neutral” on inflation.

What do political opponents say?

Jim Chalmers on Monday said the proposal was a “full-frontal attack on superannuation” and claimed it would end super “as we know it”.

Angus Taylor, the Liberal leader, said he did not want to change the way super was being paid.

The Australian Council of Trade Unions assistant secretary, Joseph Mitchell, said the proposal was the next step in Hanson’s “anti-worker” agenda.

“If Pauline Hanson wanted to help people with the cost of living, she could have backed minimum wage rises, penalty rates and safer workplaces that unions have fought for,” Mitchell said. “She voted the other way every time.”

Is super too high?

The compulsory rate of super contributions has crept up since the system was established. It sat at 9% from 2002 to 2013 and hit 12% in July 2025.

The system has generated a $4.4tn pool to fund Australians’ retirement living, reducing our reliance on the age pension. The government estimates the share of retirees receiving the full pension will fall from about 44% in 2023-24 to about 21% by 2063.

But economists have called for reform to the super system, which gives high earners big tax breaks, compounding intergenerational inequality.

The Grattan Institute estimates the current level of 12% leaves some with excess wealth and 9.5% would be enough for Australians to cover their retirement needs.

Robert Breunig, director of the Tax and Transfer Policy Institute, said One Nation’s proposal would have costs: super funds would be forced to hold more assets that can be quickly sold so they can stump up cash on demand, which could mean lower returns on workers’ investments.

Early withdrawal could worsen retirement inequality, as lower-income people would probably opt in and raid their policy while high earners keep their savings and get a bigger return, Breunig said.

But the proposal was “pushing a conversation that we probably need to have” about improving the super system.

“I think it’s just forcing people to over-save relative to what’s required,” Breunig said.

world.title: Weather tracker: Typhoon Saudel causes mass evacuations in south-east China
world.snippet: Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive hea...
world.content:
Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-east China last week. The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period. In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas. A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people.

Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region. More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas. At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes. On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing.

This is the seventh typhoon to affect China this year, and Saudel arrived shortly after Typhoon Narra dumped heavy rain on Guangdong, Hainan and Guangxi late last month.

The South African Weather Service implemented several thunderstorm warnings late last week, covering a large swathe of the northern and western provinces. Disruptive rainfall, damaging winds, excessive lightning and hail were all reported, with rainfall totals expected to have reached at least 75-100mm for parts of the Northern Cape and North West provinces over the weekend. In Johannesburg, eight families were evacuated from an apartment building after strong winds tore off a significant part of its roof.

Oppressive heat in the US affected states across the central-southern plains and the Mississippi valley this weekend, with maximum temperatures easily reaching the high 30s celsius (high 90s fahrenheit). However, with high humidities, the heat indices in this region have been closer to 40-43C (105–110F). The unrelenting temperatures will continue across the midwest and southern US this week, with maximum temperatures continuing to reach the high 30s.

world.title: Egyptian TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death for drug crime
world.snippet: Sarah Khalifa, 39, charged with forming organised criminal gang to manufacture and traffic drugs An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known...
world.content:
An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for manufacturing and trafficking narcotics in a sprawling drug case, official media reported on Saturday.

The presenter, Sarah Khalifa, 39, is best known for her programme Mission Impossible, which dealt with issues concerning security and crime.

The state-linked Al-Ahram newspaper said a Cairo court sentenced “Khalifa and 11 other defendants to death by hanging on charges of forming an organised criminal gang specialising in procuring materials used in manufacturing narcotics, with the intent to traffic them, and possessing and carrying unlicensed firearms and ammunition”.

The verdict came after the court consulted the Grand Mufti of Egypt for his religious opinion, a procedure required by Egyptian law in capital cases.

The verdict is subject to appeal.

Khalifa also owns a cosmetic surgery clinic and a production company that specialises in organising parties and events.

According to the state-run Akhbar el-Yom newspaper, the defendants were charged with “manufacturing synthetic drugs with the intent to traffic them, by importing the materials used in manufacturing from abroad”.

Al-Ahram reported that authorities seized more than 750kg of narcotics and raw materials, and found two apartments used as laboratories as well as unlicensed firearms and ammunition.

The court also sentenced Khalifa and others to five years in prison over a separate case involving the kidnapping and assault of a young man.

Egypt applies the death penalty for premeditated murder, terrorism, some rape offences and drug trafficking.

According to the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms, 541 death sentences were issued in Egypt in 2025.

world.title: UN votes to adopt new world map that shows Africa’s true scale
world.snippet: Togo-sponsored resolution called to phase out traditional map that depicts continent as similar size to Greenland The United Nations has ...
world.content:
The United Nations has voted to adopt a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe in favour of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size.

In a session at its headquarters in New York, the UN general assembly officially retired the 16th-century Mercator projection in favour of one based on the more accurate 2018 Equal Earth design.

At the session, 164 countries voted in favour of the resolution. Only the US voted no, with its representative saying the resolution was “superfluous”. There were six abstentions.

UN resolutions are non-enforceable, so countries and institutions will not be mandated to use only the new projection or forbidden from using the old one. However, the outcome is expected to result in an update of classroom curriculums and everyday technology given the wide usage of the Mercator projection in education, technology and governance.

Togo, which spearheaded a campaign for the resolution on behalf of the African Union, said the resolution “recognises and affirms that disproportionate cartographic representations, particularly those resulting from the Mercator projection, have had lasting cognitive, educational, cultural, geopolitical and socioeconomic effects, contributing to a drastic reduction in the perceived size of Africa and other regions of the world in the global collective imagination”.

Speaking before the resolution passed, Robert Dussey, Togo’s foreign affairs minister, said: “This discussion is not a political discussion [but] a scientific discussion, because there is scientific proof so we all have to accept the reality.”

The Mercator layout was introduced by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate the seas. Almost five centuries later, it remains the global standard.

Because of its projection style, however, regions near the equator appear significantly smaller than they are, whereas high-latitude areas look much larger. For example, the map shows Africa as being similar in size to Greenland, but the continent is 14 times larger than the Danish territory.

“You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare,” says a petition on Change.org for the #CorrectTheMap campaign, which has more than 11,000 signatures. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August 2025 and then asked Togo to spearhead its adoption.

On Friday, before the vote, France’s foreign minister spoke in support of the resolution. “[We] will abandon the Mercator projection in favour of map representations tailored to specific uses, more faithful to actual surface areas and in line with the recommendations of cartographers and scientists,” Jean-Noël Barrot said during a speech at the Sorbonne University in Paris, in a move seen as part of France’s push to increase goodwill among its former colonies. France will now use the Eckert IV projection, which is close to the Equal Earth projection recommended in the resolution.

Historians and geographers have said for years that the Mercator projection is rooted in western stereotypes. Activists have echoed this, with some coining the term “cartographic colonialism”.

Some argue that the map has subtly shaped international power dynamics by minimising the physical presence of the global south and visually inflating northern hemisphere nations while shrinking equatorial regions. This is said to have reinforced systemic biases in international trade, development priorities and educational frameworks.

One of the Mercator projection’s most prominent critics was Arno Peters, a German historian, who launched the Peters world map based on the Gall–Peters projection in 1973. It has often been used as an alternative to the Mercator map.

Togo’s #CorrectTheMap campaign promoted the use of the 2018 Equal Earth design, which was developed by an international team of cartographers. Supporters say it will help to reverse perceptions of Africa and decolonise global curriculums.

Some analysts agree. JJ Enoch, a London-based senior associate at JS Held, a geopolitical risk advisory firm, said the Mercator projection visually diminished Africa’s true scale. He linked the campaign to a quest by African nations for “greater influence in global institutions and greater control over how the continent is represented”.

He said: “Adopting an equal-area map … would provide a more accurate basis for education and public understanding, while signalling that Africa’s demographic, economic and geopolitical importance should no longer be viewed through inherited and distorted conventions.”

Togo’s government is planning an event in Lomé, the Togolese capital, with Unesco, the African Union and tech brands such as Google Maps during the first quarter of next year to map out the implementation of the resolution.

Speaking before the vote, Dussey said: “To those who say why now, I say: why not? When we look at the world map … it is time for us to change the narrative.”

He added: “It’s time for us in Africa to take responsibility to change what we can change ourselves.”

world.title: Spain’s PM says no evidence ‘whatsoever’ Morocco behind Ceuta border breach
world.snippet: Pedro Sánchez continues to defend Rabat after police report claiming border forces helped 70,000 cross border Europe live – latest update...
world.content:
Spain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament.

The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July.

“I ‌can assure you ‌that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, ‌nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament.

Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”.

Sánchez has repeatedly defended Morocco during the crisis, highlighting Rabat’s cooperation in returning most of the migrants in the days after the surge.

But he said on Thursday that Spain had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on 21 August because of “unacceptable statements” made by two ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish north African territory. Last month, Morocco’s justice minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, publicly reiterated Rabat’s sovereignty claims over the cities.

Sánchez said he had “for now” ruled out Moroccan government involvement but conceded that Moroccan forces had allowed crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on 30 July.

Many of those who crossed said in interviews they had been actively encouraged to do so. Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, called on Sánchez to resign for his “incompetence and complicity”.

In response to Sánchez summoning the Moroccan ambassador to discuss the crisis, Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said: “Morocco doesn’t need an ambassador in Spain – you are its ambassador.”

As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter Ceuta at the end of July. The influx unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.

On Thursday, Sánchez appealed for European solidarity over the crisis. He did not single out any countries by name but, in a pointed passage apparently aimed at Italy and Denmark, the two countries that had led public criticism of Spain, said the principle of solidarity should apply to Ceuta as much as it applies to Greenland and Lampedusa.

Although 90% of the people had returned to Morocco within 24 hours, several thousand, including at least 500 minors, are thought to remain, either living on the street or in makeshift shelters.

Amid calls from Vox to return them to Morocco, Sánchez reminded parliament that under Spanish, European and international law, migrants had a right to be treated as individuals. “You can’t just grab someone by the arm and drag them across the frontier as though they were a sack of dirt,” he told MPs.

In reference to the hundreds of destitute minors, Aina Vidal of the leftwing group Sumar, said: “They’re children, not invaders, not soldiers. They didn’t come carrying bombs, they arrived wearing water wings, in tears.”

It seems likely the government will invest in facilities in Ceuta to accommodate the remaining migrants rather than risk the political backlash both in Spain and across Europe were they to bring them to the mainland.

There is also evidence that, faced with hunger as well as hostility from many local people, some migrants have already begun going back to Morocco.

However, as Sánchez told parliament, the per capita income of Ceuta is eight times that of Morocco and “even if we build a wall 100 metres high there will still be people prepared to throw themselves into the sea to get across”.

“We will not stop working until Ceuta emerges from this difficult situation: stronger, more prosperous, and more integrated with the rest of Spain and the EU,” he added.

Additional reporting by Jakub Krupa

world.title: ‘We continue to suffer’: victims of apartheid-era Sharpeville massacre demand compensation
world.snippet: Claim relating to 1960 attack on hundreds of protesters part of wave of litigation over apartheid crimes in South Africa The day dawned b...
world.content:
The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South African township of Sharpeville gathered to protest against pass laws, which forced “Black, Indian and Coloured” South Africans to carry documents at all times specifying where they were allowed to be.

Abraham Mofokeng joined the march, one of dozens organised nationwide by the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), a breakaway group from the African National Congress (ANC). “The weather was very nice, the sun was out. You could not have suspected that the day would go so horribly,” said Mofokeng, who was then a 20-year-old factory worker.

Mofokeng, now 86, was among the thousands gathered peacefully outside the police station in Sharpeville, which is about 40 miles south of Johannesburg in a heavily industrialised region known as the Vaal Triangle.

The crowd was singing, he said, when officers opened fire without warning. At least 91 people were killed and 238 injured, in what became known as the Sharpeville massacre.

As Mofokeng fled, a bullet grazed the inside of his right foot, ripping his shoe off. A woman fell to the ground before him; he jumped over her and kept running. Only later, when he noticed blood running down his legs, did he realise he had been shot in the back, where a bullet remains lodged in his spine.

Mofokeng is among three claimants suing the South African government, in a case filed on Thursday, for compensation for the massacre. If the case is successful, dozens more could file claims.

The case is part of a wave of litigation demanding justice for apartheid-era crimes, amid widespread disillusionment with ANC-led governments that have failed to rectify South Africa’s huge racial inequality and poverty since the end of apartheid over three decades ago.

In January 2025, 25 survivors and relatives of victims of apartheid state violence sued South Africa’s government for failing to prosecute cases referred to it by the post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC). That May, the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, announced a judicial inquiry into potential political interference, which is still ongoing.

Spokespeople for South Africa’s justice department did not respond to a request for comment on the Sharpeville compensation case.

In the immediate aftermath of the Sharpeville massacre, police claimed protesters had been throwing rocks at them. “I don’t know how many we shot,” said Col J Pienaar, the local police commander, according to a story published by the Guardian the following day. “It all started when hordes of natives surrounded the police station. My car was struck with a stone. If they do these things they must learn their lesson the hard way.”

In July 1961, in response to victims filing compensation claims, the white minority regime passed a law indemnifying the government and anyone acting under its authority for any actions taken “in good faith for the prevention or suppression of internal disorder, the maintenance or restoration of good order, public safety or essential services, or the preservation of life or property”.

The law, which was made effective retrospectively from the date of the massacre, is still in force today. The claimants’ legal team is arguing that the law is unconstitutional.

The claimants are hoping to get compensation of about 500,000 rand (£23,000), said Daniel Leader, a partner with the UK law firm Leigh Day, which is advising the South African legal team, led by Lawyers For Human Rights, an NGO.

Mafokeng was awarded 30,000 rand as a one-off payment, after the TRC concluded in 2003. The TRC had recommended annual reparations payments of about 20,000 rand for six years.

“We continued to suffer,” said Mofokeng, who still lives in Sharpeville. “Especially now … I am struggling and my health is not up to standard.”

The other two test claimants were children when their fathers were killed in the massacre. Paulina Mathinye was five when her father, Samson, was shot. “Every time he came back from work, I would be so happy to see him that I would run to him, and then he would pick me up,” she said.

Mathinye did not initially understand what had happened that day in 1960. “I kept on asking my mum: ‘Mummy, why are you crying?’”

Mathinye’s mother struggled to raise her five children on a domestic worker’s wages and Mathinye, who had wanted to train as a teacher but could not afford the bursary, had to leave education at 17 to find work.

Mathinye, who is now 71, said she hoped for compensation that would make up for some of what she lost when her father died. “Some of my friends are teachers, some of them are nurses, and I’m staying in the same house that my father did,” she said.

Sharpeville’s problems did not begin with the massacre in 1960, but with the dispossession of Black South Africans from productive land, their forced removals to townships and their exclusion from the economy, said Vincent Thamae, a PAC member who supports the massacre victims and their families.

“When people talk about compensation now,” he said, “compensation is a concept to them that includes all the land that they lost, the economy that they were taken out of and even how they have been treated in the new democracy.”
